## How to read this

This is not a quickstart. It builds each method up from something small enough
to see, and the pieces arrive in the order you need them rather than the order
the API lists them.

Every figure is generated from real data by the code shown above it. Where a
number appears in the prose it came out of a cell somewhere below — if the two
ever disagree, trust the cell.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup — packages, palette, data loaders"
using DataMimic
using DataFrames, Random, Statistics, Printf, LinearAlgebra
using CairoMakie
using Lux, Zygote          # activates the DiffusionGenerator extension

include(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "benchmark", "datasets.jl"))

CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png", px_per_unit = 2)

# One restrained palette used consistently: real data is blue throughout,
# synthetic is red, and green marks the thing under discussion.
const REAL   = "#2E5E8C"
const SYNTH  = "#C4553B"
const FOCUS  = "#4F8A6B"
const MUTED  = "#9AA5B1"

set_theme!(theme_minimal();
    fontsize = 13,
    Axis = (; xgridvisible = false, ygridvisible = true,
              ygridcolor = (:black, 0.06),
              topspinevisible = false, rightspinevisible = false,
              leftspinecolor = (:black, 0.25), bottomspinecolor = (:black, 0.25)),
    Legend = (; framevisible = false))

Random.seed!(1234)
nothing
```

# 1. The problem

Start with a table you are not allowed to share.

```{julia}
adult = load_adult()
first(adult[:, [:age, :sex, :race, :marital_status, :occupation,
                :hours_per_week, :income]], 6)
```

This is the UCI Adult census extract: about 49,000 people, with age, education,
occupation, marital status, and income. Nothing in it is a name or an address.
Every direct identifier has already been stripped.

It is still not safe to publish, and the reason is worth seeing rather than
being told.

### Anonymous does not mean unidentifiable

None of these columns identifies anyone on its own. Plenty of people are 39.
Plenty are married. But *combinations* narrow very fast, and the question that
matters is how many people share your exact combination.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "How many people share your exact combination of attributes? Each bar is the share of the 48,842 records that are unique on that many columns."
# Ordered from coarse to fine, which is what makes the shape visible.
quasi = [:age, :sex, :marital_status, :occupation, :education,
         :native_country, :hours_per_week, :race]

function unique_fraction(df, cols)
    keys_ = collect(zip((df[!, c] for c in cols)...))
    counts = Dict{Any,Int}()
    for k in keys_
        counts[k] = get(counts, k, 0) + 1
    end
    count(k -> counts[k] == 1, keys_) / length(keys_)
end

ks = 1:length(quasi)
fracs = [unique_fraction(adult, quasi[1:k]) for k in ks]

fig = Figure(size = (860, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1];
    xlabel = "number of attributes known", ylabel = "share of people who are unique",
    title = "Re-identification by combination",
    xticks = (ks, string.(ks)))
barplot!(ax, ks, fracs; color = [f > 0.5 ? SYNTH : REAL for f in fracs], width = 0.65)
# The step from 6 to 7 attributes is where a fine-grained column enters.
lines!(ax, [6.5, 6.5], [0, 1.02]; color = FOCUS, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5)
text!(ax, 6.55, 0.95; text = "  + hours_per_week", align = (:left, :center),
      fontsize = 10, color = FOCUS)
for (k, f) in zip(ks, fracs)
    text!(ax, k, f + 0.02; text = @sprintf("%.0f%%", 100f),
          align = (:center, :bottom), fontsize = 10, color = :black)
end
ylims!(ax, 0, 1.08)
hlines!(ax, [0.5]; color = MUTED, linestyle = :dash)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
for k in (4, 6, 7, 8)
    @printf("%d attributes: %5.1f%% of these people are unique in the file\n",
            k, 100 * fracs[k])
end
```

Read the shape rather than any single bar. Four coarse attributes leave almost
everyone hidden in a crowd. Six still leave three quarters of people
non-unique. Then `hours_per_week` enters — a column with ninety-six distinct
values rather than a handful — and the unique share roughly doubles in one
step.

That is the mechanism worth internalising: **risk is not carried by sensitive
columns, it is carried by fine-grained ones**. Nobody would call "hours worked
per week" sensitive. It is the column that does the most damage here, because
it slices the population thinnest.

Publishing this table publishes those people. An attacker who knows seven
ordinary facts about someone — facts visible on a social media profile — can
locate their row for a coin-flip chance and read off whatever else it
contains.

### So generate new people instead

Synthetic data attacks this differently. Rather than obscuring real records, fit
a model to the table and draw *new* rows from it. Nobody in the output is
anybody in particular.

```{julia}
model = fit(CopulaGenerator(), adult; rng = MersenneTwister(1))
syn   = sample(model, nrow(adult); rng = MersenneTwister(2))
first(syn[:, [:age, :sex, :race, :marital_status, :occupation,
              :hours_per_week, :income]], 6)
```

Those rows are drawn from an estimated distribution. The 39-year-old in row 1
of the synthetic table is not the 39-year-old in row 1 of the real one.

Which raises the obvious question, and it is the one this document spends most
of its length on: **does that actually make it safe, and how would you know?**

The short answer, developed over the next four sections, is that it helps a
great deal and guarantees nothing — until you add something that does.

# 2. What is a column?

Before any model runs, every column is sorted into a kind, and almost
everything downstream turns on that decision. It is worth understanding first
because every engine in this document consumes it.

```{julia}
DataFrame(column   = Symbol.(names(adult)),
          kind     = [DataMimic.detect_column_type(adult[!, c]) for c in names(adult)],
          distinct = [length(unique(skipmissing(adult[!, c]))) for c in names(adult)],
          eltype   = [string(nonmissingtype(eltype(adult[!, c]))) for c in names(adult)])
```

Look at `:education_num`. It is stored as an integer, but it takes sixteen
values and is a coded version of `:education` — a category that happens to be
numbered. `:age` is also an integer, with seventy-four values, and is a genuine
numeric variable. Treating those two the same way would be wrong in one
direction or the other.

### The rule is cardinality, not storage type

The decision is made on how many distinct values a column holds relative to how
many rows there are — not on whether Julia stored it as an `Int`.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Each numeric column placed by its distinct-value ratio. The ones on the left have few enough levels to be categories."
numcols = [c for c in names(adult) if nonmissingtype(eltype(adult[!, c])) <: Real]
ratios = [length(unique(skipmissing(adult[!, c]))) / nrow(adult) for c in numcols]
kinds  = [DataMimic.detect_column_type(adult[!, c]) for c in numcols]

fig = Figure(size = (860, 320))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10,
    xlabel = "distinct values ÷ rows  (log scale)",
    ylabel = "", title = "Where each numeric column falls",
    yticks = (1:length(numcols), string.(numcols)),
    ygridvisible = false)
scatter!(ax, ratios, 1:length(numcols);
         color = [k === :categorical ? FOCUS : REAL for k in kinds], markersize = 14)
for (i, (r, k)) in enumerate(zip(ratios, kinds))
    text!(ax, r, i; text = "  " * string(k), align = (:left, :center),
          fontsize = 10, color = MUTED)
end
xlims!(ax, minimum(ratios) / 4, maximum(ratios) * 14)
fig
```

### Does getting it wrong actually hurt?

This is the kind of claim documentation usually asserts. It is cheap to test:
take the same table, force two columns to the wrong kind, and see what each
engine does about it.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
sub2 = adult[1:8000, [:age, :education_num, :hours_per_week, :workclass,
                      :occupation, :sex, :income]]

function typed_score(gen, hint, priv)
    hints = hint === nothing ? ColumnHint[] : [hint]
    m = fit(gen, sub2; hints = hints, privacy = priv, rng = MersenneTwister(3))
    sy = sample(m, nrow(sub2); rng = MersenneTwister(4))
    fidelity_score(sub2, sy).aggregate
end

cases = [("detected correctly",              nothing),
         ("age forced categorical",          ColumnHint(name = :age, kind = :categorical)),
         ("education_num forced continuous", ColumnHint(name = :education_num, kind = :continuous))]

DataFrame(
    typing = first.(cases),
    copula = [typed_score(CopulaGenerator(), h, nothing) for (_, h) in cases],
    mst_eps1 = [typed_score(MSTGenerator(), h, PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0))
                for (_, h) in cases],
)
```

The answer is more interesting than a flat "yes". **The copula barely notices**,
and one of the mis-typings even scores marginally better. **MST degrades by
something like forty percent.**

That difference is structural, not incidental. The copula models each column
with its *empirical* distribution, so even a column it has been told to treat
as continuous is reconstructed by interpolating between values that actually
occurred — the mistake is absorbed. MST has no such cushion: it discretizes
everything into contingency tables and then spends a finite privacy budget
measuring them. Tell it a seventy-four-level numeric column is categorical and
it now has seventy-four cells to measure with the same noise, most of them
nearly empty.

So the honest guidance is not "always check your column types". It is: the more
your engine depends on discretization, and the tighter your privacy budget, the
more the typing decision costs you. On a public copula fit you can be fairly
relaxed. On MST at ε = 1 you cannot.

### When the rule misfires

Six kinds exist: `:continuous`, `:integer`, `:categorical`, `:binary`,
`:constant`, and `:identifier`. The last is special. An identifier carries no
statistical signal but plenty of disclosure risk, so it is excluded from the
model entirely rather than synthesised — and if you give it no `fill` spec, it
is **dropped from the output**.

That is the right behaviour for a customer number. It is the wrong behaviour
for this:

```{julia}
german = load_german_credit()
DataFrame(column   = [:credit_amount, :duration_months, :age],
          kind     = [DataMimic.detect_column_type(german[!, c])
                      for c in (:credit_amount, :duration_months, :age)],
          distinct = [length(unique(german[!, c]))
                      for c in (:credit_amount, :duration_months, :age)],
          rows     = fill(nrow(german), 3))
```

`credit_amount` is a loan size in Deutschmarks — as continuous a variable as
anything in the file. But German Credit has only a thousand rows, and 921 of
the amounts are distinct. By ratio it looks exactly like a key, so it is
classified as an identifier, excluded from the model, and dropped:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
m_auto = fit(CopulaGenerator(), german; rng = MersenneTwister(11))
s_auto = sample(m_auto, 200; rng = MersenneTwister(12))
setdiff(names(german), names(s_auto))
```

This is the single most consequential way column detection goes wrong, and it
is worth internalising the shape of it: **the identifier heuristic misfires on
genuine high-cardinality columns in small datasets**, because "nearly unique"
and "is a key" look identical from a distinct-value ratio alone. The larger the
table, the safer the heuristic — a continuous column in fifty thousand rows is
rarely 92% distinct.

The fix is a hint, and every engine in this document that touches German Credit
passes one:

```{julia}
credit_hint = [ColumnHint(name = :credit_amount, kind = :continuous)]
m_hint = fit(CopulaGenerator(), german; hints = credit_hint,
             rng = MersenneTwister(11))
s_hint = sample(m_hint, 200; rng = MersenneTwister(12))
setdiff(names(german), names(s_hint))
```

The lesson generalises past this one column. Detection is a heuristic with a
silent failure mode, so **check what it decided** — the informational message
it logs is easy to miss in a long fit, and a dropped column is easy to miss in
a wide table.

# 3. Modelling a table

Now the first real method. The goal: estimate a distribution over rows, well
enough to draw new ones.

The obstacle is that a table is a *joint* distribution over columns of wildly
different types — a skewed positive number here, a sixteen-level category
there — and estimating that jointly is hard. Copulas make it tractable by
splitting the problem in two.

### Sklar's theorem: shape and dependence are separable

Any joint distribution can be written as its individual marginals, plus a
function that couples them. Formally, for a joint CDF $F$ with marginals
$F_1, \dots, F_d$ there is a copula $C$ with

$$
F(x_1, \dots, x_d) \;=\; C\bigl(F_1(x_1), \dots, F_d(x_d)\bigr),
$$

and $C$ is unique wherever the marginals are continuous.

That decomposition is exactly what tabular data wants. Each column's shape gets
modelled *exactly* by its own empirical distribution — no parametric family, no
fitting error. Only the coupling has to be estimated.

### Step one: strip the shapes away

Push each column through its own empirical CDF. Whatever it looked like, it
comes out uniform on $[0, 1]$, and only the ranks survive.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Two Wine columns before and after the rank transform. The marginal shapes are gone; the dependence is untouched."
wine = load_wine(colour = :white)

pit(v) = (sortperm(sortperm(v)) .- 0.5) ./ length(v)

fig = Figure(size = (900, 720))

ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "residual sugar", ylabel = "count",
           title = "marginal: heavily skewed")
hist!(ax1, wine.residual_sugar; bins = 60, color = (REAL, 0.75), strokewidth = 0)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xlabel = "F(residual sugar)", ylabel = "count",
           title = "after the transform: uniform")
hist!(ax2, pit(wine.residual_sugar); bins = 60, color = (FOCUS, 0.75), strokewidth = 0)

ax3 = Axis(fig[2, 1]; xlabel = "residual sugar", ylabel = "density",
           title = "joint: shape dominates the picture")
scatter!(ax3, wine.residual_sugar, wine.density;
         color = (REAL, 0.18), markersize = 4)
ylims!(ax3, 0.985, 1.005)

ax4 = Axis(fig[2, 2]; xlabel = "F(residual sugar)", ylabel = "F(density)",
           title = "joint: pure dependence")
scatter!(ax4, pit(wine.residual_sugar), pit(wine.density);
         color = (FOCUS, 0.18), markersize = 4)
fig
```

The bottom-right panel is the only thing the copula has to learn. Both axes are
uniform by construction, so nothing about the marginals remains — the visible
structure is dependence and nothing else.

### Step two: sample, then put the shapes back

Draw from the fitted copula, then push each coordinate back through the
corresponding *inverse* CDF. The marginals return exactly right by
construction, which is why copula output looks so plausible column by column.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Real against synthetic on the same axes. The dependence structure survives the round trip."
wine_model = fit(CopulaGenerator(), wine; rng = MersenneTwister(5))
wine_syn   = sample(wine_model, nrow(wine); rng = MersenneTwister(6))

fig = Figure(size = (900, 360))
for (j, (df, ttl, col)) in enumerate(((wine, "real", REAL),
                                      (wine_syn, "synthetic", SYNTH)))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; xlabel = "alcohol", ylabel = j == 1 ? "density" : "",
              title = ttl)
    scatter!(ax, df.alcohol, df.density; color = (col, 0.18), markersize = 4)
    ylims!(ax, 0.985, 1.005); xlims!(ax, 7.5, 15)
end
fig
```

### Does the whole dependence structure survive?

One scatter is anecdote. The honest check is every pair at once.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Spearman correlation across all eleven Wine columns. The third panel is the error, on a five-times tighter colour scale."
wine_cols = Symbol.(names(wine))
short(c) = (s = string(c); length(s) <= 9 ? s : s[1:8] * ".")
labels = short.(wine_cols)

spearman(df) = cor(hcat([pit(Float64.(df[!, c])) for c in wine_cols]...))
Cr, Cs = spearman(wine), spearman(wine_syn)

function corr_panel(pos, M, ttl, lims; ylabels)
    ax = Axis(pos; title = ttl, aspect = 1,
        xticks = (1:length(labels), labels),
        yticks = (1:length(labels), ylabels ? labels : fill("", length(labels))),
        xticklabelrotation = π/2, xticklabelsize = 8, yticklabelsize = 8,
        ygridvisible = false)
    heatmap!(ax, M; colormap = :RdBu, colorrange = lims)
end

fig = Figure(size = (1000, 400))
corr_panel(fig[1, 1], Cr, "real", (-1, 1); ylabels = true)
corr_panel(fig[1, 2], Cs, "synthetic", (-1, 1); ylabels = false)
Colorbar(fig[1, 3]; colormap = :RdBu, limits = (-1, 1), width = 9, label = "ρ")
hm = corr_panel(fig[1, 4], Cs .- Cr, "error (5× tighter scale)", (-0.2, 0.2);
                ylabels = false)
Colorbar(fig[1, 5], hm; width = 9, label = "Δρ")
colgap!(fig.layout, 6)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
@printf("largest correlation error: %.3f    mean: %.3f\n",
        maximum(abs.(Cs .- Cr)), mean(abs.(Cs .- Cr)))
```

### Categorical columns need one more idea

A copula wants continuous marginals. A category has none — its CDF is a
staircase, and pushing a level through it gives a single point, not a spread.

The fix is the **distributional transform**: a level occupying the CDF interval
$[F(k-1), F(k)]$ maps to a uniform draw *inside* that interval. The staircase
becomes usable, and sampling inverts the same step function.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "A categorical CDF is a staircase (left). The distributional transform spreads each level across its own step (right), which is what makes it usable as a copula coordinate."
levels_ = sort(unique(skipmissing(adult.education)))
probs = [count(==(l), skipmissing(adult.education)) for l in levels_]
probs = probs ./ sum(probs)
cdf = cumsum(probs)

fig = Figure(size = (960, 380))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; title = "empirical CDF of a 16-level column",
    xlabel = "level (ordered by index)", ylabel = "F", ygridvisible = true)
stairs!(ax1, 0:length(levels_), vcat(0.0, cdf); color = REAL, linewidth = 2.5,
        step = :post)
for (k, c) in enumerate(cdf)
    lines!(ax1, [k - 1, k], [c, c]; color = (REAL, 0.35), linewidth = 6)
end

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; title = "each level spread across its own step",
    xlabel = "uniform draw inside [F(k-1), F(k)]", ylabel = "count")
rng = MersenneTwister(9)
u = Float64[]
for (k, l) in enumerate(levels_)
    lo = k == 1 ? 0.0 : cdf[k-1]
    n = count(==(l), skipmissing(adult.education))
    append!(u, lo .+ rand(rng, n) .* (cdf[k] - lo))
end
hist!(ax2, u; bins = 80, color = (FOCUS, 0.8), strokewidth = 0)
vlines!(ax2, cdf[1:end-1]; color = MUTED, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 0.8)
fig
```

The right panel is uniform again — which is exactly what the copula needs.
Dependence between categorical and numeric columns is therefore modelled rather
than thrown away.

Two consequences follow, and they explain why there are two copula families.

The association this can express is **monotone in the level ordering**, and for
a nominal variable that ordering is arbitrary — `occupation` has no natural
sequence. So it captures a real part of the dependence, not all of it. And a
Gaussian copula has only a correlation matrix to work with, so it can express
*only* monotone dependence; the nonparametric Beta copula can represent the
non-monotone structure an arbitrary ordering produces.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
sub = adult[1:8000, [:age, :education, :occupation, :hours_per_week, :sex, :income]]
holdout = adult[8001:14000, names(sub)]

function copula_utility(kind)
    m = fit(CopulaGenerator(kind), sub; rng = MersenneTwister(7))
    s = sample(m, nrow(sub); rng = MersenneTwister(8))
    utility_tstr(sub, s, :income; test = holdout, rng = MersenneTwister(10))
end

b, g = copula_utility(:beta), copula_utility(:gaussian)
DataFrame(copula = ["beta (default)", "gaussian"],
          f1_from_synthetic = [b.synth_score, g.synth_score],
          f1_from_real      = [b.real_score,  g.real_score],
          ratio             = [b.ratio,       g.ratio])
```

On a mixed table the difference is large, and it is why `:beta` is the default.
`:gaussian` is the right choice when you specifically want a Gaussian
dependence structure — not a faster one.

### What a copula cannot do

- **Dependence is pairwise.** A three-way interaction — a relationship between
  A and B that reverses depending on C — is not represented.
- **Nominal ordering is arbitrary**, as above.
- **A single-level column** cannot be encoded at all, so it is left out of the
  copula and drawn independently.

Those limits are what the diffusion model in section 8 exists to escape. But
first, the more urgent question.

# 4. Can I publish this?

Section 3 produced a synthetic table. Every row in it is generated; none is a
copy of anyone. The natural conclusion is that it is safe to release.

Let us try to break that.

### The attack

Here is a concrete question an attacker can ask: *was Alice in the training
data?* They know Alice's attributes — age, occupation, education, hours worked
— because those are ordinary facts. They have the published synthetic table.
Nothing else.

The attack is one line of intuition. A model fitted to data containing Alice
will tend to produce synthetic rows that look slightly more like Alice than a
model fitted to data without her. So: measure how close Alice's record sits to
its nearest synthetic neighbour. If that distance is small, guess "member".

To evaluate it we need ground truth, so we fit on half the records and keep the
other half back. The attacker's score is distance-to-nearest-synthetic-row, and
we ask how well it separates the two groups.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code — Gower distance, nearest-neighbour scores, AUC"
mia_cols = [:age, :education_num, :hours_per_week, :capital_gain,
            :workclass, :education, :marital_status, :occupation, :sex, :income]
full = dropmissing(adult[:, mia_cols])
mia_num = [:age, :education_num, :hours_per_week, :capital_gain]
mia_cat = [:workclass, :education, :marital_status, :occupation, :sex, :income]

# Mixed-type distance: numeric scaled to its range, categorical 0/1 mismatch.
function encode(df, scales)
    N = Matrix{Float64}(undef, nrow(df), length(mia_num))
    for (j, c) in enumerate(mia_num)
        N[:, j] = Float64.(df[!, c]) ./ scales[j]
    end
    C = Matrix{String}(undef, nrow(df), length(mia_cat))
    for (j, c) in enumerate(mia_cat)
        C[:, j] = string.(df[!, c])
    end
    (N, C)
end

function nearest_distance(Q, S)
    (QN, QC), (SN, SC) = Q, S
    out = Vector{Float64}(undef, size(QN, 1))
    for i in axes(QN, 1)
        best = Inf
        for k in axes(SN, 1)
            d = 0.0
            @inbounds for j in axes(QN, 2); d += abs(QN[i, j] - SN[k, j]); end
            @inbounds for j in axes(QC, 2); d += QC[i, j] == SC[k, j] ? 0.0 : 1.0; end
            d < best && (best = d)
        end
        out[i] = best
    end
    out
end

# Area under the ROC curve, computed from ranks. Closer ⇒ guessed "member".
function attack_auc(d_member, d_nonmember)
    ranks = sortperm(sortperm(vcat(d_member, d_nonmember)))
    n1, n2 = length(d_member), length(d_nonmember)
    u = sum(ranks[1:n1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2
    1 - u / (n1 * n2)
end

function run_attack(n; q = 400, seed = 20)
    perm = randperm(MersenneTwister(seed), nrow(full))
    members    = full[perm[1:n], :]
    nonmembers = full[perm[n+1:n+min(n, nrow(full) - n)], :]

    m   = fit(CopulaGenerator(), members; rng = MersenneTwister(seed + 1))
    syn = sample(m, n; rng = MersenneTwister(seed + 2))

    scales = [max(maximum(Float64.(members[!, c])) -
                  minimum(Float64.(members[!, c])), 1.0) for c in mia_num]
    S  = encode(syn, scales)
    qq = min(q, nrow(members), nrow(nonmembers))
    dm = nearest_distance(encode(members[1:qq, :], scales), S)
    dn = nearest_distance(encode(nonmembers[1:qq, :], scales), S)
    (; n, auc = attack_auc(dm, dn), dm, dn)
end

attacks = [run_attack(n) for n in (500, 2_000, 10_000, 40_000)]
DataFrame(rows_fitted = [a.n for a in attacks],
          attack_auc  = [a.auc for a in attacks],
          median_member    = [median(a.dm) for a in attacks],
          median_nonmember = [median(a.dn) for a in attacks])
```

An AUC of 0.5 means the attack is guessing. Here it is not guessing.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Left: how close each real record sits to its nearest synthetic neighbour, for a model fitted to 10,000 rows. Right: the attack's accuracy against the size of the training set."
a = attacks[3]

fig = Figure(size = (960, 380))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "distance to nearest synthetic record",
    ylabel = "density", title = "fitted on 10,000 rows")
hist!(ax1, a.dm; bins = 40, normalization = :pdf,
      color = (SYNTH, 0.6), label = "in the training data")
hist!(ax1, a.dn; bins = 40, normalization = :pdf,
      color = (REAL, 0.5), label = "held out")
xlims!(ax1, 0, quantile(vcat(a.dm, a.dn), 0.97))
axislegend(ax1; position = :rt, labelsize = 10)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "rows used to fit the model",
    ylabel = "attack AUC", title = "more data does not fix it",
    xticks = ([a.n for a in attacks], string.([a.n for a in attacks])))
lines!(ax2, [a.n for a in attacks], [a.auc for a in attacks];
       color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2.5)
scatter!(ax2, [a.n for a in attacks], [a.auc for a in attacks];
         color = SYNTH, markersize = 10)
hlines!(ax2, [0.5]; color = MUTED, linestyle = :dash)
text!(ax2, first([a.n for a in attacks]), 0.52; text = "guessing",
      align = (:left, :bottom), fontsize = 10, color = MUTED)
ylims!(ax2, 0.45, 0.85)
fig
```

Two things stand out, and the second is the uncomfortable one.

The distributions genuinely separate. Records that were in the training data
sit measurably closer to the synthetic output than records that were not.

And **it does not get better with more data.** The intuition that a model
fitted to forty thousand people cannot possibly memorise any one of them is
wrong here — the attack works about as well at forty thousand rows as at five
hundred.

### Why the copula leaks

The mechanism is not subtle once you look for it, and it is a direct
consequence of the design in section 3.

The copula models each column with its **empirical** distribution. That is what
made the marginals come back exactly right. But an empirical distribution *is*
the training values — the set of ages the model can emit is precisely the set
of ages it saw, and sampling interpolates between observed values rather than
inventing new ones.

So the synthetic table is built out of real people's values, recombined.
Nobody's whole row survives, which is why no record matches exactly. But enough
of each person survives, spread across columns, for a nearest-neighbour query
to find them.

This is worth stating plainly because it generalises past this package: **a
model that reproduces your data well has, by construction, retained
information about it.** Fidelity and privacy pull in opposite directions, and
no amount of care in the modelling escapes that.

### What would fix it?

Not a better distance metric, or more rows, or a different copula family. The
problem is that we have no *bound* on how much any single record can influence
the output — we only have the observation that it seems to be a lot.

What we need is a method whose output provably barely depends on whether any
one person was in the input. That is the next section.

# 5. Differential privacy

The guarantee we want, stated before any mathematics: **if I remove you from
the dataset, the output should look essentially the same.** If that holds, then
no attacker — however clever, however well-informed — can determine whether you
were in it, because the output barely depends on the answer.

### The smallest possible example

Forget tables for a moment. Suppose I want to survey how many people have done
something they would rather not admit, and I want an honest answer.

Here is a protocol that gets one. Each respondent flips a coin in private.

- **Heads** — answer truthfully.
- **Tails** — flip again, and answer "yes" on heads, "no" on tails.

Nobody can be held to their answer. A "yes" might be true, or might be a coin.
That is *plausible deniability*, and it is built into the mechanism rather than
promised by the person collecting the data.

The remarkable part is that the aggregate survives.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Randomized response. Each individual answer is deniable, yet the population proportion is recoverable — and the estimate tightens as the sample grows."
function randomized_response(truth::AbstractVector{Bool}, rng)
    [rand(rng) < 0.5 ? t : rand(rng) < 0.5 for t in truth]
end

# Half the answers are noise with mean 1/2, so:  observed = p/2 + 1/4
recover(observed_rate) = 2 * observed_rate - 0.5

true_p = 0.30
rng = MersenneTwister(77)
sizes = round.(Int, exp10.(range(2, 5; length = 22)))
ests = [recover(mean(randomized_response(rand(rng, n) .< true_p, rng))) for n in sizes]

fig = Figure(size = (960, 360))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "what one person reports", ylabel = "",
    title = "an individual answer says almost nothing",
    yticks = ([1, 2], ["truth = no", "truth = yes"]), ygridvisible = false)
for (row, p_yes) in ((1, 0.25), (2, 0.75))
    barplot!(ax1, [row - 0.0], [p_yes]; direction = :x, width = 0.45,
             color = (SYNTH, 0.85))
    barplot!(ax1, [row - 0.0], [1 - p_yes]; direction = :x, width = 0.45,
             color = (REAL, 0.35), offset = p_yes)
    text!(ax1, p_yes / 2, row; text = @sprintf("says yes %.0f%%", 100p_yes),
          align = (:center, :center), fontsize = 10, color = :white)
end
xlims!(ax1, 0, 1)
ax1.xlabel = "probability"

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "respondents",
    ylabel = "estimated proportion", title = "the aggregate is recoverable")
hlines!(ax2, [true_p]; color = FOCUS, linewidth = 2, label = "truth = 0.30")
scatter!(ax2, sizes, ests; color = SYNTH, markersize = 7)
lines!(ax2, sizes, ests; color = (SYNTH, 0.4))
axislegend(ax2; position = :rt, labelsize = 10)
ylims!(ax2, 0, 0.6)
fig
```

Someone who reports "yes" is only three times more likely to have meant it than
not. That ratio — how much more probable your true answer makes the observed
one — is the entire idea. Differential privacy is that ratio, bounded and
named.

### The definition, now that it is obvious

A mechanism $M$ is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differentially private if for any two
datasets $D$ and $D'$ differing in a single record, and any set of outputs $S$:

$$
\Pr[M(D) \in S] \;\le\; e^{\varepsilon}\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] \;+\; \delta .
$$

Read it as: *removing one person changes the probability of any outcome by at
most a factor of $e^{\varepsilon}$*. The coin-flip protocol above satisfies this
with $\varepsilon = \ln 3 \approx 1.1$.

$\delta$ is an escape hatch — a small probability that the bound fails
outright. It should stay well below $1/n$; at $\delta \approx 1/n$ a mechanism
is permitted to publish a whole record now and then and still call itself
private. DataMimic defaults it to `1e-5`.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "What ε permits. The shaded band is the range of output probabilities compatible with the guarantee once one record changes — narrow at small ε, effectively unconstrained by ε = 10."
eps_grid = range(0.01, 5; length = 300)
base = 0.30

fig = Figure(size = (860, 360))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "ε", ylabel = "probability of the same outcome",
    title = "how much can one person change the answer?")
band!(ax, eps_grid, base .* exp.(-eps_grid), min.(base .* exp.(eps_grid), 1.0);
      color = (SYNTH, 0.18))
lines!(ax, eps_grid, min.(base .* exp.(eps_grid), 1.0); color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2)
lines!(ax, eps_grid, base .* exp.(-eps_grid); color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2)
hlines!(ax, [base]; color = FOCUS, linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash,
        label = "without you: 0.30")
for (e, lbl) in ((0.5, "strict"), (1.0, "common"), (3.0, "weak"))
    vlines!(ax, [e]; color = MUTED, linewidth = 0.8)
    text!(ax, e, 0.96; text = "  " * lbl, align = (:left, :top),
          fontsize = 10, color = MUTED)
end
axislegend(ax; position = :lt, labelsize = 10)
ylims!(ax, 0, 1)
fig
```

At $\varepsilon = 0.5$ your presence can move any probability by at most about
65% in relative terms. At $\varepsilon = 3$ it can move it twentyfold, which is
not much of a promise. This is why the number matters and why quoting it
without context is meaningless.

### Three properties that make it usable

**Sensitivity sets the noise.** To release a statistic privately you add noise
scaled to how much one record could change it. A count changes by at most 1, so
counts are cheap. A sum of unbounded values could change by anything, so it
must be clipped first. Every mechanism in this package is an instance of this
pattern.

**Composition is additive, and it is a budget.** Answer two private questions
and the privacy loss adds up. This is the part practitioners underestimate:
$\varepsilon$ is not a setting per query, it is a *total* to be divided across
everything the algorithm does. DataMimic composes under zero-concentrated DP
(zCDP), which is tighter than naive addition across many mechanisms.

**Post-processing is free.** Anything computed from a private output is still
private, with no further cost. This is not a technicality — it is what makes
synthetic data work at all. Once the model is private, you can draw a thousand
rows or a million from it without spending anything more, and everything
downstream inherits the guarantee.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "How each engine divides a single budget across the steps it must take. Nothing here is free except the reconciliation and the sampling."
splits = [
    ("MSTGenerator", ["select tree" => 0.30, "1-way marginals" => 0.20,
                      "2-way marginals" => 0.50]),
    ("DPCopulaGenerator", ["histogram marginals" => 0.50,
                           "private covariance" => 0.50]),
]
fig = Figure(size = (880, 260))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "share of the total ε budget", ylabel = "",
    yticks = (1:length(splits), first.(splits)), ygridvisible = false,
    title = "Where the budget goes")
palette = [REAL, FOCUS, SYNTH]
for (row, (_, parts)) in enumerate(splits)
    off = 0.0
    for (k, (label, frac)) in enumerate(parts)
        barplot!(ax, [row], [frac]; direction = :x, width = 0.5,
                 offset = off, color = (palette[k], 0.85))
        text!(ax, off + frac / 2, row; text = label, align = (:center, :center),
              fontsize = 10, color = :white)
        off += frac
    end
end
xlims!(ax, 0, 1)
fig
```

### What it costs

Nothing is free. The noise that buys the guarantee also degrades the output,
and the only way to know by how much on *your* data is to measure it.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The privacy–utility curve on German Credit. Steep at the left, flat at the right — the useful question is where your data stops improving."
eps_grid2 = [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0]

sweep = privacy_utility_sweep(MSTGenerator(), german, eps_grid2,
            (r, s) -> fidelity_score(r, s).aggregate;
            hints = credit_hint, rng = MersenneTwister(31))
vals = [r.metric_result for r in sweep]

public = let m = fit(CopulaGenerator(), german; hints = credit_hint,
                    rng = MersenneTwister(32))
    fidelity_score(german, sample(m, nrow(german); rng = MersenneTwister(33))).aggregate
end

fig = Figure(size = (860, 360))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, xlabel = "ε  (log scale)",
    ylabel = "fidelity distance  (lower is better)",
    title = "what a privacy budget costs",
    xticks = (eps_grid2, string.(eps_grid2)))
lines!(ax, eps_grid2, vals; color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2.5)
scatter!(ax, eps_grid2, vals; color = SYNTH, markersize = 9)
hlines!(ax, [public]; color = REAL, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2,
        label = "no privacy at all")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

The gap between the curve and the dashed line is the price of the guarantee.
It shrinks as ε grows, and — importantly for later — it also shrinks as the
dataset grows, because the noise is fixed by sensitivity while the signal is
not.

With the idea in place, the next three sections are about how each engine
spends a budget.

# 6. Private copulas

The copula from section 3 has two parts: the marginals and the dependence.
Making it private means making both private, and each needs a different
mechanism.

### Private marginals

A marginal is a histogram — a set of counts. Counts are the friendliest thing
in differential privacy, because one person changes a count by exactly one.
Sensitivity is 1, so noise is cheap.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The same histogram released at three budgets. Noise is added to every bin, so small bins are the ones that suffer."
counts = [count(==(l), skipmissing(adult.workclass))
          for l in sort(unique(skipmissing(adult.workclass)))]
labs = sort(unique(skipmissing(adult.workclass)))

fig = Figure(size = (980, 330))
for (j, eps) in enumerate((0.1, 1.0, Inf))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j];
        title = isinf(eps) ? "no noise" : "ε = $eps",
        xticks = (1:length(labs), string.(labs)),
        xticklabelrotation = π/4, xticklabelsize = 8,
        ylabel = j == 1 ? "count" : "")
    noisy = isinf(eps) ? counts :
            counts .+ randn(MersenneTwister(40 + j), length(counts)) .* (2 / eps)
    barplot!(ax, 1:length(labs), max.(noisy, 0);
             color = isinf(eps) ? (REAL, 0.85) : (SYNTH, 0.85))
    hlines!(ax, [0]; color = MUTED, linewidth = 0.8)
end
fig
```

Notice what the noise does and does not damage. The large categories are barely
affected — adding a few dozen to a count of thirty thousand is nothing. The
small ones are wrecked, and can even go negative before clamping.

That is the general shape of differential privacy on real data: **it taxes the
rare much more heavily than the common**. Which is a reasonable thing for a
privacy mechanism to do, since rare is exactly what makes someone identifiable
— but it means minority groups in your data lose the most fidelity, and that is
worth knowing before you publish.

### Private dependence: Analyze-Gauss

The dependence half is a covariance matrix, and the mechanism for releasing one
privately is **Analyze-Gauss** (Dwork, Talwar, Thakurta & Zhang, 2014): clip
the rows to bound their influence, form the second-moment matrix, and add
Gaussian noise.

One detail there is easy to get wrong and silently halves your protection. A
covariance matrix is symmetric, so the noise added to it must be symmetric
too — draw the upper triangle and mirror it across the diagonal. Noising both
triangles independently gives every off-diagonal entry *half* the intended
variance, and the guarantee you claim no longer holds.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Wine's correlation structure at three budgets. The strong relationships survive; the weak ones dissolve into noise first."
wnum = Matrix{Float64}(wine[:, Symbol.(names(wine))])
C0 = cor(wnum)

fig = Figure(size = (1000, 300))
for (j, eps) in enumerate((0.5, 2.0, Inf))
    M = if isinf(eps)
        C0
    else
        r = MersenneTwister(50 + j)
        E = randn(r, size(C0)...) .* (0.35 / eps)
        E = (E .+ E') ./ 2                    # symmetric noise, as above
        clamp.(C0 .+ E, -1, 1)
    end
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; aspect = 1,
        title = isinf(eps) ? "no noise" : "ε = $eps",
        xticksvisible = false, yticksvisible = false,
        xticklabelsvisible = false, yticklabelsvisible = false,
        ygridvisible = false)
    heatmap!(ax, M; colormap = :RdBu, colorrange = (-1, 1))
end
Colorbar(fig[1, 4]; colormap = :RdBu, limits = (-1, 1), width = 9, label = "ρ")
fig
```

Put the two halves together and you have `DPCopulaGenerator`: private
histograms for the marginals, a private covariance for the coupling, and half
the budget for each.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
dpc = fit(DPCopulaGenerator(), wine;
          privacy = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0), rng = MersenneTwister(51))
dpc_syn = sample(dpc, nrow(wine); rng = MersenneTwister(52))

DataFrame(engine = ["CopulaGenerator (no guarantee)", "DPCopulaGenerator (ε = 1)"],
          fidelity = [fidelity_score(wine, wine_syn).aggregate,
                      fidelity_score(wine, dpc_syn).aggregate])
```

This is the engine for continuous-heavy data, and Wine is exactly that shape. A
covariance matrix is a natural summary of eleven correlated measurements. It is
a poor summary of nine unordered categories — which is what the next section is
for.

# 7. MST: privacy for discrete data

MST won the NIST differential privacy synthetic data challenge. Its central
idea is a budgeting one: **you cannot afford to measure everything, so spend
the budget on the relationships that matter most.**

Consider a table with $d$ columns. There are $d$ one-way marginals and
$\binom{d}{2}$ two-way ones. Measuring all of them privately splits the budget
so many ways that each measurement is pure noise. Measuring none of the
two-way marginals loses every relationship. MST measures a carefully chosen
few.

### The six steps

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
# credit_amount needs the hint from section 2, or it is treated as an
# identifier and dropped.
mst_model = fit(MSTGenerator(), german; hints = credit_hint,
                privacy = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0, delta = 1e-5),
                rng = MersenneTwister(60))
mst_syn = sample(mst_model, nrow(german); rng = MersenneTwister(61))
first(mst_syn[:, [:checking_status, :duration_months, :purpose,
                  :credit_amount, :age, :credit_risk]], 5)
```

1. **Discretize.** Everything becomes bins — numeric columns into 32
   equal-width bins by default — because the algorithm works over contingency
   tables. This is why column typing mattered so much in section 2.
2. **Measure every one-way marginal** under Gaussian noise. There are only $d$
   of them, so they are cheap, and they anchor each column's own distribution.
3. **Choose a spanning tree.** Score each candidate pair by how badly the
   independence assumption fails for it, then pick a maximum spanning tree over
   columns using the **exponential mechanism** — which makes the *choice
   itself* private, not just the measurements.
4. **Measure the chosen two-way marginals** under Gaussian noise. A tree over
   $d$ columns has exactly $d - 1$ edges, so this is $d - 1$ measurements
   rather than $\binom{d}{2}$.
5. **Reconcile.** The noisy measurements contradict each other — one marginal's
   implied column totals will not match another's. Private-PGM fits a single
   tree-structured graphical model that best explains all of them at once.
6. **Sample** ancestrally down the tree, then map bins back to values.

Step 5 is **post-processing**: it touches only already-private numbers, so it
costs nothing. That is the property from section 5 doing real work.

### Why a tree?

This is the choice that makes the whole thing tractable, and it is worth
seeing why.

A general graph of dependencies requires approximate inference — you cannot
compute the implied joint distribution exactly, so reconciliation becomes an
approximation on top of noisy data. A **tree** has no cycles, which means
belief propagation is exact and terminates in two passes. You give up the
ability to represent some dependency structures, and in exchange every step
afterwards is exact and cheap.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code — laying out the selected tree"
#| fig-cap: "The dependency tree the exponential mechanism selected. Because selection is private, a different seed gives a different tree — read it as one plausible skeleton, never as discovered structure."
names_ = string.(mst_model.stat_columns)
edges = mst_model.tree_edges
root = mst_model.root

# Depth-first placement: children are spread beneath their parent.
children = Dict{Int,Vector{Int}}()
for (p, c) in edges
    push!(get!(children, p, Int[]), c)
end

order = Int[]
depth = Dict{Int,Int}()
function walk(v, d)
    push!(order, v); depth[v] = d
    for c in get(children, v, Int[]); walk(c, d + 1); end
end
walk(root, 0)

xpos = Dict(v => i for (i, v) in enumerate(order))
maxd = maximum(values(depth))

fig = Figure(size = (1000, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; title = "selected dependency tree (German Credit, ε = 1)",
    xticksvisible = false, xticklabelsvisible = false,
    yticksvisible = false, yticklabelsvisible = false,
    ygridvisible = false, xgridvisible = false,
    leftspinevisible = false, bottomspinevisible = false)
for (p, c) in edges
    lines!(ax, [xpos[p], xpos[c]], [-depth[p], -depth[c]];
           color = (MUTED, 0.8), linewidth = 1.4)
end
for v in order
    scatter!(ax, [xpos[v]], [-depth[v]];
             color = v == root ? SYNTH : REAL, markersize = 13)
    text!(ax, xpos[v], -depth[v] - 0.16; text = names_[v],
          align = (:center, :top), fontsize = 8,
          rotation = π/6, color = :black)
end
ylims!(ax, -maxd - 1.2, 0.6)
xlims!(ax, 0, length(order) + 1)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
@printf("%d columns, %d edges measured — instead of %d possible pairs.\n",
        length(names_), length(edges), binomial(length(names_), 2))
```

That ratio is the whole argument. Measuring every pair would divide the budget
more than four times as many ways, and each measurement would be
correspondingly noisier.

### Where MST is strong, and where it is not

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The same two engines on two shapes of data, both at ε = 1. Each is better at exactly what the other is not."
function fid(gen, df, priv, seed; hints = ColumnHint[])
    m = fit(gen, df; hints = hints, privacy = priv, rng = MersenneTwister(seed))
    fidelity_score(df, sample(m, nrow(df); rng = MersenneTwister(seed + 1))).aggregate
end

b1 = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0)
results = DataFrame(
    dataset = ["German Credit (14 categorical)", "Wine (11 continuous)"],
    MST     = [fid(MSTGenerator(), german, b1, 62; hints = credit_hint),
               fid(MSTGenerator(), wine, b1, 64)],
    DPCopula = [fid(DPCopulaGenerator(), german, b1, 63; hints = credit_hint),
                fid(DPCopulaGenerator(), wine, b1, 65)],
)
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-cap: "Lower is better. The ordering reverses between the two datasets."
fig = Figure(size = (760, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "fidelity distance (lower is better)",
    xticks = (1:2, results.dataset), title = "matching the engine to the shape")
barplot!(ax, [0.82, 1.82], results.MST; width = 0.34, color = (REAL, 0.85),
         label = "MSTGenerator")
barplot!(ax, [1.18, 2.18], results.DPCopula; width = 0.34, color = (SYNTH, 0.85),
         label = "DPCopulaGenerator")
axislegend(ax; position = :lt, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

This is the clearest engine-selection result in the document, and it is the one
that actually holds up: on discrete data MST wins, on continuous data the DP
copula wins, and the margin is large in both directions. Discretizing eleven
continuous measurements into bins throws away most of what makes them
informative; summarising nine unordered categories with a covariance matrix
does the same in the other direction.

# 8. Diffusion

The copula assumes dependence has a particular shape. MST assumes it factors
along a tree. A diffusion model assumes almost nothing and learns the
distribution instead — at the cost of far more data and compute.

The idea is a strange one and worth stating carefully: **destroy the data
gradually, learn to undo one step of the destruction, then start from pure
noise and undo your way back to a sample.**

### The forward process

Add a little Gaussian noise at each of $T$ steps. With
$\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s\le t}(1 - \beta_s)$, you can jump straight to any step:

$$
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\bigl(x_t;\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_t)\mathbf{I}\bigr).
$$

So $\bar\alpha_t$ is the whole schedule: how much of the original signal
survives to step $t$.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "A real column dissolving. By t = 100 nothing of the original distribution is left — which is the point, because that is where sampling starts."
const Ext = Base.get_extension(DataMimic, :DataMimicLuxExt)
T = 100
betas_cos, _ = Ext._cosine_schedule(T)
sched = Ext._schedule_constants(betas_cos)

x0 = Float32.((adult.age .- mean(adult.age)) ./ std(adult.age))[1:6000]
fig = Figure(size = (1000, 240))
for (j, t) in enumerate([1, 25, 60, 100])
    ab = sched.alphas_cumprod[t]
    xt = sqrt(ab) .* x0 .+ sqrt(1 - ab) .* randn(MersenneTwister(t), Float32, length(x0))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title = "t = $t    ᾱ = $(round(ab; digits = 3))",
        yticksvisible = false, yticklabelsvisible = false, ygridvisible = false)
    hist!(ax, xt; bins = 60, color = (j == 1 ? REAL : FOCUS, 0.8), strokewidth = 0)
    xlims!(ax, -4, 4)
end
fig
```

The schedule controls how that dissolution is paced, and the choice matters:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The cosine schedule destroys signal gradually. The linear one collapses it early and then spends most of its steps on noise that is already noise."
betas_lin = collect(range(1e-4, 0.02; length = T))
ac_lin = cumprod(1 .- betas_lin)

fig = Figure(size = (900, 320))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "timestep t", ylabel = "ᾱₜ (signal retained)",
    title = "how much of x₀ survives")
lines!(ax, 1:T, sched.alphas_cumprod; color = FOCUS, linewidth = 2.5,
       label = "cosine (used)")
lines!(ax, 1:T, ac_lin; color = MUTED, linewidth = 2.5, linestyle = :dash,
       label = "linear")
axislegend(ax; position = :rt, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

### Two processes at once

Gaussian noise makes no sense for a categorical column — there is nothing
between "married" and "divorced" to interpolate through. TabDDPM therefore
runs a **second diffusion process in parallel, over the same timestep**.

Multinomial diffusion interpolates each one-hot vector toward the uniform
distribution over its levels:

$$
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathrm{Cat}\bigl(x_t;\ (1-\beta_t)\,x_{t-1} + \beta_t/K\bigr).
$$

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Categorical diffusion: a one-hot vector melting toward uniform over its five levels. The reverse process learns to sharpen it back."
K = 5
fig = Figure(size = (1000, 220))
for (j, t) in enumerate([1, 30, 65, 100])
    ab = Float64(sched.alphas_cumprod[t])
    p = fill((1 - ab) / K, K); p[2] += ab      # level 2 was the true one
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title = "t = $t",
        xticks = (1:K, ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]),
        ylabel = j == 1 ? "probability" : "", ygridvisible = true)
    barplot!(ax, 1:K, p; color = [i == 2 ? FOCUS : MUTED for i in 1:K])
    ylims!(ax, 0, 1.05)
end
fig
```

Carrying this in **log space** is not an optimisation but a necessity:
probabilities for a 42-level column at $t = 100$ underflow `Float32` otherwise.

### What the network learns

Training samples a random $t$ per row, noises the row to that step, and asks
the network to predict the noise that was added. The objective is plain squared
error for the numeric half and a KL divergence against the true posterior for
the categorical half.

Then sampling runs the whole thing backwards, one step at a time.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code — this is the one slow cell in the document"
adult_sub = adult[1:20_000, [:age, :workclass, :education, :marital_status,
                             :occupation, :hours_per_week, :sex, :income]]

diff_t0 = time()
diff_model = fit(DiffusionGenerator(epochs = 150, batch_size = 4096,
                                    d_layers = [256, 512, 512, 256],
                                    num_timesteps = 100, target = :income),
                 adult_sub; rng = MersenneTwister(70))
diff_secs = time() - diff_t0
diff_syn = sample(diff_model, nrow(adult_sub); rng = MersenneTwister(71))

cop_m = fit(CopulaGenerator(), adult_sub; rng = MersenneTwister(72))
cop_s = sample(cop_m, nrow(adult_sub); rng = MersenneTwister(73))

DataFrame(engine = ["CopulaGenerator", "DiffusionGenerator (150 epochs)"],
          fidelity = [fidelity_score(adult_sub, cop_s).aggregate,
                      fidelity_score(adult_sub, diff_syn).aggregate],
          fit_seconds = [NaN, diff_secs])
```

**The copula wins, comfortably, and that result should not be read as a verdict
on diffusion.** One hundred and fifty epochs over twenty thousand rows at batch
4096 is roughly seven hundred optimizer steps. The configuration in the TabDDPM
paper uses several thousand, on a network about four times wider. This document
trains a small model because it has to render in a reasonable time.

The failure is visible in the numeric columns, and it has a specific cause:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
DataFrame(column = [:age, :hours_per_week],
          real_sd  = [std(adult_sub.age), std(adult_sub.hours_per_week)],
          synth_sd = [std(diff_syn.age),  std(diff_syn.hours_per_week)])
```

The reverse process divides by $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$, which reaches the order of
$10^3$ at the noisiest steps of a 100-step cosine schedule. Any error in the
predicted noise is amplified by that factor, so an imperfectly trained model
produces numeric columns that are far too spread out. Train it properly and
this closes; the mechanism is what to understand here, not the number.

### Making it private: ghost clipping

DP-SGD clips **each example's** gradient to a fixed norm before adding noise.
That per-example clipping is what bounds one person's influence — and it looks
like it requires a separate backward pass per example, which would be
catastrophic.

It does not. For a dense layer with inputs $a$ and output-gradients $g$,
example $i$'s weight gradient is an outer product $g_i a_i^\top$, so its norm
factorises:

$$
\bigl\|\partial L_i/\partial W\bigr\|_F \;=\; \|g_i\|\,\|a_i\| .
$$

Two column norms. Sum them across layers and you have every example's gradient
norm — hence its clip factor — without ever forming a per-example gradient. The
clipped sum is then two more matrix multiplications. Two batched passes replace
$B$ unbatched ones.

This is **ghost clipping**, and it is an exact identity rather than an
approximation. In this package it took DP-SGD from 73.2 to 0.42 seconds per
epoch on the same configuration, and the test suite asserts the two routes
agree to floating-point rounding.

# 9. Evaluation

Three families of metric, measuring three different things, and the interesting
cases are where they disagree.

- **Fidelity** — do the distributions match?
- **Utility** — does a model trained on it work on real data?
- **Privacy** — how close does it sit to real records?

### Why fidelity alone is not enough

Start with the trap, because it explains the shape of everything else.

Here is a deliberately broken generator: take the real table and shuffle every
column independently. Each column's marginal is now *perfect* — it is the real
marginal, exactly. Every relationship between columns has been destroyed.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
shuffled = DataFrame()
for (i, c) in enumerate(names(adult_sub))
    shuffled[!, c] = shuffle(MersenneTwister(80 + i), adult_sub[!, c])
end

f_shuf, f_cop = fidelity_score(adult_sub, shuffled), fidelity_score(adult_sub, cop_s)

DataFrame(
    generator = ["column-shuffled (deliberately broken)", "CopulaGenerator"],
    per_column = [mean(values(f_shuf.column_scores)),
                  mean(values(f_cop.column_scores))],
    correlation = [f_shuf.correlation_score, f_cop.correlation_score],
    aggregate = [f_shuf.aggregate, f_cop.aggregate],
    pairwise_error = [pairwise_marginal_error(adult_sub, shuffled).mean,
                      pairwise_marginal_error(adult_sub, cop_s).mean],
    tstr = [utility_tstr(adult_sub, shuffled, :income;
                         rng = MersenneTwister(81)).ratio,
            utility_tstr(adult_sub, cop_s, :income;
                         rng = MersenneTwister(81)).ratio],
)
```

Read the first two columns against each other. On **per-column** distance the
broken generator is essentially perfect — its marginals are not approximations
of the real ones, they *are* the real ones. A metric that looked only at
marginals would rank it top.

The **correlation** column is where it falls apart, and that term is what drags
its aggregate below the copula's despite those flawless marginals. The two
downstream measures agree: five times the pairwise marginal error, and a
utility ratio of about 0.57 against the copula's 1.0.

So the aggregate does catch it — but only because it is not purely marginal.
That is the design point worth taking away: **any evaluation built solely on
per-column comparisons can be passed by a generator that has destroyed every
relationship in your data.** Check a dependence-aware measure, and check
utility if you can define a task.

### Fidelity, in detail

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
f = fidelity_score(adult_sub, cop_s)
@printf("aggregate           %.4f   (0 = perfect)\n", f.aggregate)
@printf("correlation term    %.4f\n", f.correlation_score)
@printf("columns compared    %d   excluded %d\n",
        length(f.correlation_columns), length(f.correlation_excluded))
sort(DataFrame(column = collect(keys(f.column_scores)),
               distance = collect(values(f.column_scores))), :distance, rev = true)
```

Every number is a **distance**, so lower is better. Numeric columns use the
Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic — the largest vertical gap between the two
empirical CDFs — and categorical columns use total variation distance. Both are
bounded in $[0, 1]$, which is what makes them commensurable enough to average.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "The KS statistic is a single number with a picture: the widest vertical gap between two empirical CDFs."
vr = sort(Float64.(adult_sub.age)); vs = sort(Float64.(cop_s.age))
grid = range(minimum(vr), maximum(vr); length = 500)
ecdf(v) = [count(<=(x), v) / length(v) for x in grid]
Fr, Fs = ecdf(vr), ecdf(vs)
k = argmax(abs.(Fr .- Fs))

fig = Figure(size = (760, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "age", ylabel = "F(age)",
    title = @sprintf("KS = %.4f", maximum(abs.(Fr .- Fs))))
lines!(ax, grid, Fr; color = REAL, linewidth = 2.5, label = "real")
lines!(ax, grid, Fs; color = SYNTH, linewidth = 2.5, label = "synthetic")
lines!(ax, [grid[k], grid[k]], [Fr[k], Fs[k]];
       color = FOCUS, linewidth = 3, label = "KS")
scatter!(ax, [grid[k], grid[k]], [Fr[k], Fs[k]]; color = FOCUS, markersize = 8)
axislegend(ax; position = :rb, labelsize = 10)
fig
```

The correlation term compares **Spearman** rather than Pearson correlation,
deliberately: rank correlation is invariant to the marginal shapes already
scored by the per-column terms, so the two halves measure different things
instead of double-counting.

### Utility

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
u = utility_tstr(adult_sub, cop_s, :income; rng = MersenneTwister(82))
DataFrame(task = [string(u.task)], f1_from_synthetic = [u.synth_score],
          f1_from_real = [u.real_score], ratio = [u.ratio])
```

Train on synthetic, test on real. Gradient-boosted trees are fitted twice —
once on synthetic data, once on real — and both are scored against the same
held-out real data. The ratio is the number that matters, and it is the most
direct evidence that a synthetic table is fit for anything.

One caution that recurs later: ratios slightly above 1 are common and do not
mean synthetic data beats real data. Both scores are noisy, and their ratio is
noisier.

### Privacy

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Distance to the closest real record. The degenerate case on the right is what memorisation looks like."
d_syn  = privacy_dcr(adult_sub[1:3000, :], cop_s[1:3000, :])
d_copy = privacy_dcr(adult_sub[1:3000, :], adult_sub[1:3000, :])

@printf("synthetic      median DCR %.4f, exact matches %d\n",
        d_syn.median, d_syn.exact_matches)
@printf("real vs itself median DCR %.4f, exact matches %d\n",
        d_copy.median, d_copy.exact_matches)

fig = Figure(size = (760, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "distance to closest real record",
    ylabel = "density", title = "DCR distribution")
hist!(ax, d_syn.dcr; bins = 50, normalization = :pdf,
      color = (SYNTH, 0.75), strokewidth = 0)
vlines!(ax, [d_syn.median]; color = FOCUS, linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash)
text!(ax, d_syn.median, 0.0; text = "  median", align = (:left, :bottom),
      fontsize = 10, color = FOCUS)
fig
```

`exact_matches` should be zero. The second line is the degenerate case for
comparison: a table scored against itself has every distance zero and every row
an exact match, which is what a generator that memorised its input would look
like.

Treat DCR as a smoke test, not a guarantee. Section 4 already showed the
limitation concretely — the copula there had no exact matches at all and still
leaked membership at AUC 0.72. **A good DCR does not substitute for a privacy
budget.**

# 10. How these break

Documentation usually stops at the happy path. These are the failure modes that
actually occur, all of them found by running the code rather than reading it.

### An undertrained diffusion model over-disperses

Section 8 showed this. The mechanism is worth restating because the symptom is
distinctive: the reverse process divides by $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$, of order
$10^3$ at the noisiest steps, so any error in the predicted noise is amplified
by the same factor. Numeric columns come out far too wide.

If your synthetic numeric columns have two or three times the standard
deviation of the real ones, the model is undertrained. It is not a
hyperparameter to tune away; it is a signal to train longer.

### Rejection sampling is not distribution-preserving

When the reverse process overflows, the offending rows are discarded and
redrawn. That sounds harmless. It is not.

Keeping only the rows that come back finite samples from the distribution
*conditioned on finiteness* — and divergence is not independent of the data.
For a class-conditional model it correlates with the **label**, because the
label is an input to the denoiser. On an undertrained Adult model this turned a
76/24 income split into 100% a single class, in a table that otherwise looked
entirely well-formed.

DataMimic now tracks the discard rate and refuses rather than returning a
biased sample:

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code — deliberately undertraining to trip the guard"
tiny = adult[1:4000, [:age, :hours_per_week, :workclass, :education, :income]]
result = try
    m = fit(DiffusionGenerator(epochs = 2, batch_size = 512,
                               d_layers = [32, 32], num_timesteps = 100,
                               target = :income, lr = 5e-3),
            tiny; rng = MersenneTwister(90))
    s = sample(m, 2000; rng = MersenneTwister(91))
    income_split = [count(==(l), s.income) / nrow(s)
                    for l in sort(unique(tiny.income))]
    "sampled — income split $(round.(income_split; digits = 3))"
catch e
    "refused — " * first(split(sprint(showerror, e), '\n'))
end
println(result)
println("real split: ",
        round.([count(==(l), tiny.income) / nrow(tiny)
                for l in sort(unique(tiny.income))]; digits = 3))
```

Whether that cell samples or refuses depends on how badly this particular tiny
model diverges. Either outcome is the point: you get a usable sample or an
error, never a quietly skewed table.

### Seed variance can exceed the difference you are measuring

At tight privacy budgets, the same engine on the same data gives visibly
different answers run to run.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Ten fits of the same engine on the same data, differing only in seed. Each dot is one run; the bar is the mean."
function seed_spread(eps, seeds)
    [begin
        m = fit(MSTGenerator(), german; hints = credit_hint,
                privacy = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = eps), rng = MersenneTwister(s))
        fidelity_score(german, sample(m, nrow(german); rng = MersenneTwister(s + 1))).aggregate
     end for s in seeds]
end

seeds = 100:109
lo, hi = seed_spread(0.5, seeds), seed_spread(4.0, seeds)

fig = Figure(size = (760, 340))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "fidelity distance", xticks = (1:2, ["ε = 0.5", "ε = 4.0"]),
    title = "ten seeds, identical settings")
for (x, vals, col) in ((1, lo, SYNTH), (2, hi, REAL))
    scatter!(ax, fill(x, length(vals)) .+ 0.06 .* randn(MersenneTwister(1), length(vals)),
             vals; color = (col, 0.8), markersize = 11)
    lines!(ax, [x - 0.2, x + 0.2], fill(mean(vals), 2); color = col, linewidth = 3)
end
fig
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
@printf("ε = 0.5: mean %.4f, sd %.4f\n", mean(lo), std(lo))
@printf("ε = 4.0: mean %.4f, sd %.4f\n", mean(hi), std(hi))
@printf("\nFor scale, the MST/DPCopula gap on this dataset in section 7 was %.4f.\n",
        abs(results.MST[1] - results.DPCopula[1]))
```

The absolute spread is larger at the tighter budget, which is the expected
direction — more noise is being injected. But the number to hold onto is the
last line: **one standard deviation of seed-to-seed variation is a substantial
fraction of the engine-to-engine differences you are usually trying to
detect.**

That is why `compare` repeats every engine over several seeds and warns below
three. A single-seed comparison of two private engines is measuring noise as
much as method.

### Numerical failures hide in log space

The categorical machinery works in log space, and log-space code fails in ways
that produce `NaN` rather than an obviously wrong number.

One real example from this package: the per-block log-softmax subtracted a
single **global** maximum before exponentiating. With raw network logits
spanning roughly ±100, a block sitting far below the global maximum underflowed
to zero across all its rows — so the block sum was 0, `log(0)` was `-Inf`, and
the whole loss became `NaN`. It required both several categorical columns and a
wide batch to appear, which is why it survived a long time. The fix was a
per-block maximum.

The general lesson: **a numerical bug in log space is invisible until it is
catastrophic.** If training produces `NaN`, suspect an underflow before
suspecting the learning rate.

# 11. Choosing an engine, measured

Everything above describes what each engine is *for*. This section tests
whether that description predicts anything.

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
function bench(df, target; hints = ColumnHint[], n = 4_000, seeds = 3)
    sub = df[1:min(n, nrow(df)), :]
    compare([CopulaGenerator(), CopulaGenerator(:gaussian),
             MSTGenerator(), DPCopulaGenerator()], sub;
            metrics = (fidelity = (r, s) -> fidelity_score(r, s).aggregate,
                       utility  = (r, s) -> utility_tstr(r, s, target;
                                                rng = MersenneTwister(95)).ratio),
            n_seeds = seeds, hints = hints,
            privacy = PrivacyBudget(epsilon = 1.0),
            rng = MersenneTwister(96))
end

results_all = vcat(
    (d = DataFrame(bench(german, :credit_risk; hints = credit_hint));
     d.dataset .= "German Credit"; d),
    (d = DataFrame(bench(wine, :quality)); d.dataset .= "Wine"; d),
    (d = DataFrame(bench(adult_sub, :income)); d.dataset .= "Adult"; d),
)
select(results_all, :dataset, :generator, :metric, :mean, :sd, :fit_secs)
```

```{julia}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#| fig-cap: "Fidelity by engine and dataset (lower is better). The two private engines are paying for a guarantee the two public ones do not provide."
fid_rows = filter(r -> r.metric === :fidelity && r.ok, results_all)
gens = unique(fid_rows.generator)
dsets = unique(fid_rows.dataset)
cols4 = [REAL, "#7FA6C9", FOCUS, SYNTH]

fig = Figure(size = (900, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; ylabel = "fidelity distance (lower is better)",
    xticks = (1:length(dsets), dsets), title = "same four engines, three datasets")
w = 0.8 / length(gens)
for (gi, g) in enumerate(gens)
    xs, ys, es = Float64[], Float64[], Float64[]
    for (di, d) in enumerate(dsets)
        r = filter(x -> x.generator == g && x.dataset == d, fid_rows)
        isempty(r) && continue
        push!(xs, di + (gi - (length(gens) + 1) / 2) * w)
        push!(ys, r.mean[1]); push!(es, isnan(r.sd[1]) ? 0.0 : r.sd[1])
    end
    barplot!(ax, xs, ys; width = w * 0.88, color = (cols4[gi], 0.9), label = g)
    errorbars!(ax, xs, ys, es; color = :black, whiskerwidth = 6)
end
axislegend(ax; position = :lt, labelsize = 9)
fig
```

### What this actually shows

**The public copula wins on fidelity everywhere, and that is not a finding
about algorithm quality.** `CopulaGenerator` is not solving the same problem as
`MSTGenerator` — it offers no privacy guarantee at all. Comparing them on
fidelity measures the *price of privacy*, which is the honest way to read that
chart. The gap is what a formal guarantee costs on your data.

**Among engines that solve the same problem, shape predicts the winner.**
Section 7 made this comparison properly: at the same ε, MST wins on the
categorical dataset and the DP copula wins on the continuous one, in both
directions by a clear margin. That is the one selection rule in this document
that survived testing.

**The `:beta` / `:gaussian` split flips with the data.** Beta wins on the
categorical-heavy tables, where an arbitrary level ordering produces
non-monotone structure only a nonparametric copula can represent. Gaussian is
competitive on all-continuous Wine, where a single correlation matrix is close
to the right model.

**The error bars are not decoration.** Where they overlap, the difference in
means is not evidence of anything — and a single-seed run would have reported a
confident winner regardless.

### Practical guidance

**Start with `CopulaGenerator()`.** Seconds to fit, strong on mixed types, and
it gives you the baseline everything else has to beat. If it is good enough,
you are done.

**Decide whether you need a guarantee before you start.** Privacy cannot be
retrofitted — a non-private model has already seen the data, and no amount of
post-hoc checking changes that. Section 4 is the argument for deciding this
deliberately rather than by inspection.

**Match the private engine to the data shape.** Discrete → MST. Continuous →
DP copula. This is the one shape-based rule the measurements support.

**Give every engine a fair configuration.** A diffusion model at a small epoch
count measures your patience, not the method.

**Use at least three seeds**, and read the spread before the mean.

**Check what column detection decided.** It is a heuristic with a silent
failure mode, and a dropped column is easy to miss.
